title: Regional cancer centre: pragmatic trial of automatic palliative care referral triggers, empty searches confirmed and a certainty from leads dropped
notes: Demanding path with nothing retrieved. The need names a pragmatic trial (clinics switching in a staggered order) and gives local volumes, capacity and approval facts; the problem reply restates the investigator's constraints exactly (G11). The first fixture search returns HTTP 200 with zero records, recorded as an event with 0 hits. A discovery reply over those zero records brings five model leads and a certainty 'moderate': the certainty must be dropped with an issue and the Scan stays incomplete with the honest status 'leads only' (G1, G2); the leads are stored as unverified model leads, and the two undated leads keep year and quality null and grade unrated, never 2020, 50 or 'low' (G3, G4). The investigator runs a broader second search, which is recorded and also empty, and then confirms the empty search on screen: only that confirmation completes the Scan, it is stored as an investigator action, and certainty stays unassessed (not assessed on screen and in the export). With no ledger claim, the design decision narrows the proposal to one stepped-wedge trial with one primary outcome; its ethics gate has no evidence and stays unknown, so acceptance gives an accepted selection with a blocked action, which is checked again after a reload on the Design route at 7 of 13 stages. Requires D20 (drop of a certainty over zero records, leads-only status, investigator confirmation record, not assessed on screen), S11 (explicit basis, recommendedFamily, selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text). Catches: a certainty assigned or a Scan completed from leads or an empty search, a model or an empty result treated as the investigator's confirmation, invented defaults for unknown values, a gate that becomes met without evidence, an action allowed past an unknown ethics gate, and work lost on reload or reopen.

inputs.need:
I am a palliative medicine physician at a regional cancer centre that sees about 1,900 new patients with advanced solid tumours each year across eight disease-site clinics. Referral to our specialist palliative care clinic depends on the treating oncologist, and it comes late: last year the median time from the first palliative care visit to death was 34 days, and a third of patients who died under our care were never seen by palliative care at all.

We would like to test automatic referral triggers built into the electronic health record. A referral would be generated when a patient meets any of a small set of criteria (for example a new diagnosis of stage IV lung, pancreatic or gastric cancer, the start of second-line chemotherapy, two unplanned admissions within 60 days, or a documented performance status of 3 or worse) unless the oncologist opts the patient out. Usual care would stay as it is now, with referral at the oncologist's discretion.

We are thinking of a pragmatic trial in which the clinics switch from usual care to the triggers in a staggered order over about 18 months, so that every clinic eventually gets the triggers. The main questions are whether triggers bring the first palliative care visit earlier, whether patients spend more days at home in their last months, and whether our palliative care team can cope with the extra referrals. Some oncologists worry that automatic referrals will upset patients who are not ready and will swamp the palliative care clinic.

I need help with the choice of primary outcome, the trigger criteria, how many clinics and patients we need, how to handle clinics that switch at different times, and the ethics of automatic referral with an opt-out.
inputs.constraints: The palliative care team can add 0.5 full-time equivalent nurse time and no physician time. Trigger rules can be built in the electronic health record from the first quarter of 2027. Outcomes must come from routinely collected data; no extra questionnaires for patients who are very unwell.
localFacts: The centre sees about 1,900 new patients with advanced solid tumours a year across eight disease-site clinics.
In 2025 the median time from the first specialist palliative care visit to death was 34 days, and 33 percent of patients who died under the centre's care had no palliative care visit.
The palliative care outpatient clinic can see about 30 new patients a week.
The medical oncology division agreed on 2026-09-10 to take part with opt-out automatic referral in all eight clinics (division minutes MO-2026-09-10).
The research ethics board has not yet reviewed the proposal.

response.rationale: Every clinic will receive the triggers, the intervention changes how referral happens, and the outcomes can come from routine records, so a pragmatic stepped-wedge trial in the eight clinics answers the question under real conditions. Randomising the order in which pairs of clinics switch protects against the clinic differences a before-after comparison would carry, and period effects are modelled. Nothing was retrieved, so the design rests on the investigator's local facts and on stated assumptions rather than on appraised evidence.
alternatives: Before-after comparison across the centre (refused: changes in referral practice over time would be confounded with the triggers)
Parallel cluster trial with four clinics kept on usual care throughout (refused: the division agreed to triggers in all eight clinics, and a stepped rollout protects clinic capacity)
Individually randomised trial (refused: triggers act at the clinic level, and patients of the same oncologist would contaminate each other)
guidelines: CONSORT extension for stepped-wedge cluster randomised trials

store.title: Automatic referral triggers for early specialist palliative care in outpatient oncology: a pragmatic stepped-wedge trial

response.overview: Pragmatic stepped-wedge trial in the eight disease-site clinics: after a 3-month baseline, pairs of clinics switch from usual referral to opt-out automatic referral triggers every 3 months, in an order randomised by the trial statistician, until all eight use triggers after 15 months; outcomes come from routine records with 90 days of follow-up.
response.population: Adults aged 18 and over with an advanced solid tumour under the care of one of the eight clinics who meet at least one trigger criterion during the trial periods; the first trigger per patient defines entry. Patients already known to specialist palliative care or enrolled in hospice care are excluded.
response.exposure: An automatic referral to the specialist palliative care clinic generated by the electronic health record when a trigger is met (new stage IV lung, pancreatic or gastric cancer; start of second-line systemic therapy; two unplanned admissions within 60 days; documented performance status 3 or worse), sent unless the oncologist opts the patient out within 5 working days; compared with usual referral at the oncologist's discretion.
response.procedures: Informatics builds and tests the trigger rules before the first step and runs them silently in usual-care periods, so eligible patients are identified the same way in both conditions. In trigger periods the palliative care nurse calls each referred patient to explain the referral and offer an appointment; the patient may decline. Opt-outs and declines are recorded with a reason. Outcomes are extracted from admission, clinic and death records by an analyst who does not see the step schedule until the analysis.

outcomes.why: The direct effect of the triggers; shows whether a null result reflects no change in referral.

outcomes.why: Care that patients with advanced cancer often do not want.

outcomes.why: Extra referrals could lengthen waits for patients who need care most.

parsimony.simplestPath: One primary outcome from routine data, one pre-specified mixed model, and eight clinics in four steps.

response.theoreticalFramework: None; the question is the effectiveness of a referral change under usual conditions. An implementation framework is left to a later process evaluation.
response.summary: Stepped-wedge trial in eight clinics over five periods; one primary outcome, one secondary, one process and one balancing measure.

response.designSummary: Cross-sectional stepped-wedge cluster trial: eight clinics, four steps of two clinics, five 3-month periods, patients nested in clinic-periods.
response.sampleSize: About 120 patients a month are expected to meet a trigger (an assumption from the centre's volumes, to confirm on 2025 records), about 45 per clinic in each 3-month period and about 1,800 in total. For days alive and out of hospital in 90 days the planning values are a standard deviation of 24 days and an intracluster correlation of 0.03. With eight clinics switching in four pairs over five periods, a standard stepped-wedge calculation with exchangeable correlation gives about 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a difference of about 5.5 days. A smaller difference would need more clinics rather than more patients per clinic, because the clinic-level correlation limits the gain from larger clusters; a correlation that decays over time would lower power and is examined as a sensitivity calculation.
response.primaryAnalysis: Linear mixed model for days alive and out of hospital with fixed effects for period and condition (triggers versus usual referral) and random intercepts for clinic and clinic-period, adjusted for age, tumour group and trigger type; the effect is a mean difference in days with a 95 percent confidence interval, analysed by the condition of the clinic when the patient first met a trigger.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Mixed logistic model for a first palliative care visit within 12 weeks; aggressive end-of-life care among patients who die within 12 months; waiting time described by month; opt-out and decline rates by clinic.
response.missingData: Outcomes come from linked records and are expected to be complete for admissions and deaths within the region; patients who move away are censored at last contact, and their number is reported by condition.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary, process and balancing outcomes reported with confidence intervals and labelled as such.
response.software: R with the lme4 package; the sample size recalculated with a stepped-wedge calculator once the 2025 trigger volume is known.
overfittingGuards: Primary outcome, covariates and model fixed in a statistical analysis plan before the first step
Period effects always in the model
No subgroup claims beyond tumour group and trigger type
Sample size assumptions checked on 2025 records before the first step
response.summary: About 1,800 patients in eight clinics give about 80 percent power for a 5.5-day difference in days alive and out of hospital.

response.risks: An unrequested referral may distress patients who are not ready to hear about palliative care, and extra referrals may lengthen waits for patients already referred; the trial adds no procedures.
response.consent: The trigger changes how referral is offered, and every patient can decline the appointment when the palliative care nurse calls. The research ethics board will be asked to approve an alteration of consent for the referral process and a waiver for routinely collected outcome data, with information posters in every clinic.
response.data: Outcome data are extracted within the hospital's secure environment; the analysis file carries study identifiers only; clinic results are shared with oncologists without naming individual clinicians.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients who live far from the centre, patients who need an interpreter, patients from communities where palliative care is associated with giving up, and patients with low health literacy may respond differently to an automatic referral. Calls use interpreters, telehealth appointments are offered, and uptake and outcomes are reported by distance, language and area deprivation.
response.effectiveness: The trial shows whether triggers change time at home and end-of-life care, not only when referral happens.
response.efficiency: Routine data and existing staff plus the added nurse time; the trigger build is a one-time informatics task.
response.costs: Added nurse time and the informatics build within the centre's budget; no payments to participants.
response.grants: A regional cancer research grant could fund the analysis and a later process evaluation; the trial can run without it.
response.partnerships: Medical oncology division, informatics, two patient partners with experience of advanced cancer, a family caregiver partner and the community hospice.
response.rebPath: Full research ethics board review of a stepped-wedge cluster trial with an alteration of consent for automatic referral and a waiver for routine outcome data, following ICH-GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki. The board has not yet reviewed the proposal, so the gate stays unknown and no trigger goes live before its decision.
response.limitations: Eight clusters limit power for small effects; oncologists may change behaviour before their clinic switches; routine data miss symptom burden and quality of life.
response.summary: Minimal added risk, an opt-out referral with the right to decline, consent alteration to be decided by the board, and equity reporting by distance, language and deprivation.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners and a family caregiver review the call script and the information posters before the first step; oncologists from two clinics and the palliative care nurse join the oversight group that reviews waiting times monthly.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the centre's patient feedback forms from the last year are read for comments about palliative care referral.

response.title: Opt-out automatic referral triggers for early specialist palliative care in outpatient oncology: protocol and results of a pragmatic stepped-wedge trial
response.abstract: Background: referral to specialist palliative care is late at a regional cancer centre. Design: pragmatic stepped-wedge trial in eight clinics switching in randomised pairs from usual referral to opt-out automatic referral triggers over five 3-month periods. Primary outcome: days alive and out of hospital in the 90 days after trigger eligibility, from routine records. Results and conclusions will be written after the trial.
response.introduction: Palliative care delivered alongside oncology treatment is associated with less aggressive end-of-life care in recalled studies, but referral depends on individual oncologists and is often late. Automatic triggers could make referral systematic; two recorded searches found no evaluation of outpatient opt-out triggers.
response.methods: Eligible patients are identified by the same electronic rules in both conditions. Referrals in trigger periods are sent unless the oncologist opts out within 5 working days. A linear mixed model with period and clinic effects estimates the difference in days alive and out of hospital.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present clinic flow by period, trigger volume, opt-outs and declines, the primary estimate with its confidence interval, the process, secondary and balancing outcomes, and results by distance, language and deprivation.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the estimate against time trends and capacity, compare it with the literature once it has been retrieved and checked, and state what the centre will do with the triggers.
response.limitations: Eight clusters; possible contamination before switching; routine data without symptom or quality-of-life measures; evidence base not yet retrieved.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am a palliative medicine physician at a regional cancer centre that sees about 1,900 new patients with advanced solid tumours each year across eight disease-site clinics. Referral to our specialist palliative care clinic depends on the treating oncologist, and it comes late: last year the median time from the first palliative care visit to death was 34 days, and a third of patients who died under our care were never seen by palliative care at all.

We would like to test automatic referral triggers built into the electronic health record. A referral would be generated when a patient meets any of a small set of criteria (for example a new diagnosis of stage IV lung, pancreatic or gastric cancer, the start of second-line chemotherapy, two unplanned admissions within 60 days, or a documented performance status of 3 or worse) unless the oncologist opts the patient out. Usual care would stay as it is now, with referral at the oncologist's discretion.

We are thinking of a pragmatic trial in which the clinics switch from usual care to the triggers in a staggered order over about 18 months, so that every clinic eventually gets the triggers. The main questions are whether triggers bring the first palliative care visit earlier, whether patients spend more days at home in their last months, and whether our palliative care team can cope with the extra referrals. Some oncologists worry that automatic referrals will upset patients who are not ready and will swamp the palliative care clinic.

I need help with the choice of primary outcome, the trigger criteria, how many clinics and patients we need, how to handle clinics that switch at different times, and the ethics of automatic referral with an opt-out.
